Caching reasoning from core utilities to Next.js layers

nodes.norm_label: note: this file should not be edited

nodes.label: apps/angular-lab (Angular 20, standalone, zoneless)
nodes.rationale: Deliberately ships no zone.js at all, using provideZonelessChangeDetection(), because signals-plus-zoneless is the highest-leverage Angular differentiator few candidates can speak to credibly.

nodes.label: Problem: design system for many teams
nodes.norm_label: problem: design system for many teams
nodes.rationale: Tokens to CSS custom properties to components on headless primitives so accessibility is not re-litigated per component; the trap is over-abstracting before three products' worth of real usage.

nodes.label: 2026 senior posting signals
nodes.rationale: Drawn from a sweep of senior job ads; the strategic read is that Next.js is the highest-leverage fluency for React roles while Angular is the highest-leverage differentiator because fewer candidates can speak to signals and zoneless.

nodes.label: The prep kit (docs index)
nodes.rationale: Ordered live coding first, system design second, theory third, even though the folders are numbered by topic, because that ordering matches where interview loops actually fail candidates.

nodes.label: Re-render diffing vs signal dependency graph
nodes.norm_label: re-render diffing vs signal dependency graph
nodes.rationale: React's granularity is the component and identity is manual (key, memo, dep arrays); Angular's granularity is the expression and the graph handles identity but is easier to wire so nothing updates. The two are converging via the React Compiler and standalone/inject().

nodes.label: Zoneless change detection
nodes.rationale: Zone.js monkey-patched every async browser API and checked the whole tree, which is why Angular felt magic and was slow by default. Zoneless checks a view only on signal change, input change, template event, markForCheck, or async pipe emission; it is essentially OnPush everywhere, enforced.

nodes.label: Read doc comment, close, rebuild, diff
nodes.norm_label: read doc comment, close, rebuild, diff
nodes.rationale: The labs are not to be read as documentation: implement from the description, then diff, because the gaps are the study list. Source comments are written as interview answers — what to say out loud and what the follow-up will be.

nodes.label: useSyncExternalStore and tearing
nodes.rationale: Concurrent rendering makes tearing possible with external stores; the selector must be stable or getSnapshot changes identity every render and loops forever, which is why Redux ships a with-selector variant.

nodes.label: Angular hierarchical DI vs React context
nodes.norm_label: angular hierarchical di vs react context
nodes.rationale: The injector walks root to route to element, giving route-scoped lifetimes, InjectionToken, multi providers and @Self/@SkipSelf control that React context cannot do as cleanly. Nest shares the decorator syntax but is module-scoped and needs exports.

nodes.label: NestJS request lifecycle order
nodes.rationale: middleware to guards to interceptors to pipes to handler and back out through interceptors and exception filters; the order answers 'where would you put X?' — authz in a guard, validation in a pipe, logging in an interceptor, error envelope in a filter.

nodes.label: Problem: collaborative editor
nodes.rationale: CRDT versus OT, WebSocket with presence, local-first via IndexedDB, and per-user undo; the trap is treating it as a save problem when it is a merge problem.

nodes.label: Store + undo/redo demo
nodes.rationale: useSyncExternalStore versus subscribe-to-signal, to demonstrate what state libraries actually are underneath.

nodes.label: Context has no selector
nodes.rationale: Every consumer re-renders when the value changes and there is no selector, so split contexts by update frequency or use an external store — precisely why Zustand and Jotai exist.

nodes.label: Keys as identity claims
nodes.rationale: Index keys attach state to position rather than item, which is fine for static lists and a bug for reorderable ones; deliberately changing a key is the cleanest way to reset state.

nodes.label: useEffect as synchronisation, not lifecycle
nodes.rationale: If a value can be computed during render, an effect is the wrong tool; the three anti-patterns are deriving state in an effect, fetching without cancellation, and resetting state on prop change instead of using a key.

nodes.label: DTO validation with whitelist
nodes.rationale: DTOs must be classes because decorators need runtime metadata; whitelist plus forbidNonWhitelisted is the pairing that actually blocks mass assignment. zod via nestjs-zod is the modern alternative giving one schema for validation and inference.

nodes.label: Polling vs SSE vs WebSocket
nodes.rationale: SSE is the cheapest correct answer for one-way feeds because it rides HTTP and auto-reconnects; choose WebSocket only when you need to write, since it needs its own scaling and backoff logic.

nodes.label: packages/core (framework-agnostic logic)
nodes.rationale: Kept framework-agnostic and consumed from dist/ so both labs share one implementation and the 18 unit tests double as the live-coding drill specs.

nodes.label: satisfies operator
nodes.rationale: as lies to the compiler and a type annotation widens; satisfies checks without widening, so config.port stays number.

nodes.label: Three kinds of state (server, URL, client)
nodes.norm_label: three kinds of state (server, url, client)
nodes.rationale: Server state to a query cache, URL state to the URL, client state local until genuinely shared — naming the three kinds is the senior answer to 'what state management would you pick?'.

nodes.label: Graceful shutdown and AsyncLocalStorage
nodes.rationale: On SIGTERM stop accepting, drain in-flight and close pools (what enableShutdownHooks does in nest-api main.ts); AsyncLocalStorage carries a request id through async calls for log correlation.

nodes.label: Client-to-CDN caching stack
nodes.rationale: Browser HTTP cache to CDN to app data cache to in-memory client cache; stale-while-revalidate is the single most useful header to mention, and on the client an LRU with TTL plus request dedup (LruCache and singleFlight in packages/core).

nodes.label: Error handling and resilience
nodes.rationale: Boundaries per route and per widget so one failure does not blank the page; retry with exponential backoff and jitter (retry() in packages/core); circuit-break a failing dependency; always offer a recovery affordance.

nodes.label: Tier 1 vanilla JS/TS drills
nodes.rationale: debounce, throttle, LRU, emitter, promisePool, retry with jitter, singleFlight, observable store, undo/redo and Result — each paired with the follow-up question interviewers actually ask.

nodes.label: 45-minute system design framework
nodes.rationale: Requirements, non-functional targets, architecture, data flow, module design, deep dive, trade-offs. Scoping before solving and closing with what you gave up and how you would know it was wrong is the part most candidates skip and the most senior-sounding.

nodes.label: How to behave in a live session
nodes.norm_label: how to behave in a live session
nodes.rationale: Half the score. Restate constraints first to avoid solving the wrong thing well; naive version first because working at minute 15 beats perfect at minute 40; offer a test because almost nobody does and it changes the read on you.

nodes.label: Reactive forms and ControlValueAccessor
nodes.rationale: Reactive forms are the senior answer because validation is explicit, testable and composable; template-driven ngModel is fine for two fields and hard to test.

nodes.label: Next.js four caching layers
nodes.rationale: Request memoization, Data Cache, Full Route Cache, Router Cache; revalidatePath/revalidateTag invalidate the middle two. Naming all four separates 'I've used Next' from 'I understand Next'. In 15 fetch is no longer cached by default and cookies/headers/params are async.

nodes.label: Problem: checkout / multi-step form
nodes.rationale: URL-driven steps, client validation for UX and server for truth, idempotency key on submit, draft persisted locally; optimistic UI is wrong here because payment needs a confirmed result.

nodes.label: Nest vs Next, when to choose
nodes.norm_label: nest vs next, when to choose
nodes.rationale: Next is a frontend framework with a server, good for BFF-shaped work; Nest is a backend framework with modules, DI, jobs, queues and a domain layer. The common production shape is both.

nodes.label: Server Actions are public endpoints
nodes.rationale: 'use server' exposes each exported function as a public POST endpoint, so authorization and validation must happen inside the action — hiding a button in the UI is not authorization.

nodes.label: 'use client' as a boundary
nodes.rationale: The directive is a boundary not a file marker — everything imported beneath it also ships to the browser — so keep the page a Server Component, push 'use client' to the smallest interactive leaf, and pass server content down as children.

nodes.label: Conditional type distributivity
nodes.rationale: T extends U ? X : Y distributes over a naked union parameter; wrapping in a tuple switches it off.

nodes.label: unknown vs any vs never
nodes.rationale: any switches the checker off and is contagious; unknown forces narrowing (as attempt() does with e instanceof Error); never is the bottom type used for exhaustiveness via assertNever.

nodes.label: Node event loop phases
nodes.rationale: timers, pending callbacks, poll, check, close; nextTick and promise microtasks drain between every phase with nextTick first. Blocking the single thread is the cardinal sin — CPU work goes to worker_threads or off the box.

nodes.label: Streams and backpressure
nodes.rationale: stream.pipeline handles backpressure and also propagates errors and cleans up; streaming a CSV keeps memory O(1) instead of O(file).

nodes.label: Branded ProductId type
nodes.rationale: TypeScript is structural, so two same-shaped string ids are interchangeable; an intersection with a phantom __brand property fakes nominal typing so getProduct(userId) stops compiling.

nodes.label: RemoteData discriminated union
nodes.rationale: Four booleans allow 16 states, 12 of which are nonsense; a discriminated union makes 'loading with data present' unrepresentable.

nodes.label: Problem: dashboard with live data
nodes.rationale: One multiplexed connection rather than twenty, per-widget Suspense and error boundaries, coalesced updates and server-side aggregation; the trap is re-rendering the whole grid on every tick.

nodes.label: Problem: news feed / infinite scroll
nodes.rationale: Cursor pagination, virtualisation, optimistic likes, prefetch n+1, scroll restoration from history state; the trap is unreserved image dimensions failing CLS.

nodes.label: Product table demo
nodes.rationale: useReducer + useMemo versus signal + computed — picked to expose derived state, memoisation and coupled state invariants such as filter changes resetting the page.

nodes.label: Virtual list demo
nodes.rationale: Same scroll/slice/spacer maths in both frameworks, so the only difference visible is how the derived slice is recomputed; the point is rendering 50k rows without jank.

nodes.label: When to memoise
nodes.rationale: useMemo/useCallback are hints React may discard; memoise only for genuinely expensive computation or where identity feeds another hook or a memo'd child. The React Compiler makes manual memoisation largely legacy for pure components.

nodes.label: Ordered React performance checklist
nodes.rationale: Stated in order (measure, fix state location, cut work, cut re-renders, cut bundle, concurrent features) because saying it in order shows optimisation by measurement rather than reflex. Targets: INP < 200 ms, LCP < 2.5 s, CLS < 0.1.

nodes.label: Testing house style (role queries, userEvent)
nodes.rationale: Query by role and accessible name so tests exercise the accessibility tree too; test behaviour not implementation. Fake timers with userEvent need advanceTimers, the answer to 'my test hangs'.

nodes.label: Offset vs cursor pagination
nodes.rationale: Offset is simple but breaks under concurrent inserts as rows shift and items duplicate or vanish; cursor/keyset is stable for infinite scroll and high-write tables but cannot jump to page 47.

nodes.label: RxJS flattening operators
nodes.rationale: Signals have no concept of time, so event streams still want RxJS. switchMap cancels (the typeahead default), mergeMap parallelises, concatMap preserves order, exhaustMap guards double-submit.

nodes.label: Problem: typeahead at scale
nodes.rationale: Debounce 200-300 ms, cancel in flight, LRU cache by query prefix, minimum query length, dedup, keyboard support and aria-live count; the trap is the race condition, implemented twice in this repo.

nodes.label: Typeahead race condition
nodes.rationale: A stale response overwriting a newer one is the single bug the drill exists to expose; fixed with AbortController in React and switchMap in Angular.

nodes.label: Tier 2 React component drills
nodes.rationale: Each drill is indexed by the specific bug being checked for: uncleaned timers, the stale-response race, filter not resetting the page, missing overscan, hooks-based error boundary, unstable selector loops, ref written during render, re-subscribing listeners.

nodes.label: Tier 3 Angular equivalents
nodes.rationale: Named the highest-value exercise in the repo: write the Angular version of a demo from memory after closing the React one, then the reverse.

nodes.label: Typeahead demo
nodes.rationale: Chosen because it forces race conditions, cancellation and cleanup into the open: React solves it with useDebouncedValue + AbortController, Angular with debounceTime + switchMap and again with resource().

nodes.label: Drill workflow (blank file, timer, diff)
nodes.rationale: Read only the description, implement blank against a timer, run the repo's existing tests as your spec, then diff — the tests exist first so the drill has an objective pass condition.

nodes.label: Four twinned demos (React vs Angular)
nodes.rationale: The same four components are built twice on one framework-agnostic core so the only remaining difference is the reactivity model — that isolates exactly what interviewers probe when they ask whether a React developer can do Angular or vice versa.
